units.title: Account status: no liabilities past due
units.author: grieve_payroll
units.text: Account status notice. Reference: GLS-KH-0001-S01. Status: no employee-day liabilities on this site account are past due at the time of this notice. Liabilities raised tonight will fall due at the end of the following workday as usual. This is an automated message. Please do not reply to this address; replies are not monitored.

units.author: sam
units.text: anyway mum's hip. the doctor's letter came and they're talking about doing it properly in a few weeks, the operation, not just the exercises. she says she's 'not fussed', which means she's fussed. I've said I'll take her in and Jamie has offered to 'help the doctors', which I've declined on everyone's behalf. you don't need to do anything, I just thought you'd want to know. go to bed. love again, S x

units.author: sb_bins
units.text: I see from the council notices that the van 'may arrive later in the morning than the usual lorry'. I see from my window that the usual lorry has not arrived in the morning for three weeks. So the van will arrive later than never. I have put this in my log, page four. Bernard (Rope Walk)

units.author: dc_3_wendell
units.text: Bernard, page four. I admire a man who numbers his pages. My own letters to Kerrow Estates are now in a ring binder with dividers, one colour per fault. The lift is red. The bins are green. The stairwell lights now have a yellow divider of their own, which tells you how this week has gone.

units.author: sb_mod
units.text: For what it's worth, Bernard, my waste team contact says the van is real, it has been seen, and it will do Rope Walk on Thursday 'if the chapel end is clear of parked cars'. So if anyone on Rope Walk owns a car, the chapel end on Thursday morning is a place you should not be.

units.author: sb_roadworks
units.text: 06:10 this morning: frost on the reservoir bridge, gritter had been through, bless it. Lights fine on the way out. Radio says they stuck again at 07:50 towards Port Ammet, fifteen-minute queue, a listener 'learned a lot about the cones'. That listener wasn't me but it could have been. We are all cone scholars now.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Ours were in the 07:50 queue. My eldest counted forty-one cones and then started naming them. Number seventeen is called Derek. I've asked the school whether the bus will run if the fog's bad tomorrow and they said 'at the driver's discretion', which I'll be honest is not as reassuring as they think.

units.author: sb_commuter_lisle
units.text: Lisle 07:15 on time, sea like glass. Fog advisory from tonight, the bulletins say, so I have packed a book, a scarf and a second sandwich in anticipation of a long morning. Last fog week I sat outside Gilliver for thirty-five minutes listening to the horn and reading the safety card in three languages.

units.author: retired_teacher
units.text: Ewan, a book, a scarf and a second sandwich is the most sensible packing you have done since your Year Six residential, when you brought a bag of marbles and one sock. Do take a torch tomorrow. The walk up from the Lisle slip in fog is worse than the crossing, and the lamp at the top has been out since the summer.

units.author: ferry_engineer_seth
units.text: Thirty-five minutes outside Gilliver was me waiting for the skipper to be sure of the slip. You can't see the end of it in proper fog; you just have to trust the radar and the lamps. It's slow because it's supposed to be slow. Bring the second sandwich. Bring a third, I'll have it.

units.author: retired_teacher
units.text: I have a bolt of blue cotton left over from the Lisle school's production of Noah, which, I'm afraid, was 1997. It has been in a cupboard since then, but it was a good, dry cupboard. I can bring it over on the ferry on Saturday if someone can meet me at Port Ammet with a car.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Mrs Hale, you are a saint. I'll meet you off the ferry on Saturday with the car and a flask. The director said 'oh thank goodness' out loud when I told her, which I've never heard a teacher say in front of children before. The river will finally be blue. The Bulrushes are thrilled, as far as Bulrushes can be.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Dinosaur glove reunited! A grandad from the estate came into the pharmacy holding the other one and asked if I was 'the glove woman'. I am now the glove woman. The adult sock and the hair bobble remain unclaimed on the bakery railing. Awake_at_3, I think they're yours to curate now.

units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: I accept the post of curator. The sock has been there four nights now, through two frosts, and has developed a certain dignity. I'll give it until the end of the week and then bring it into the shop, where it can sit in the window with the other things nobody came back for.

units.author: sb_bins
units.text: Checked the sheds and the bin store along Rope Walk at first light. No cat. One aggrieved gull in the bin store, which I have spoken to. I have also asked the van driver, when he exists, to look under his vehicle before he moves off. Bernard (Rope Walk)

units.author: trades_holm_work
units.text: Checked the lock-up at six, behind every drum and under the van. No Pebble, sorry. Found a hedgehog asleep in a coil of rope, so I've left the rope where it is and the door open a crack. If a grey cat turns up I'll ring the number on your poster straight away.

units.author: sb_lostcat
units.text: Still no Pebble. I've knocked on fourteen doors and looked in more sheds than I knew existed in Port Ammet. Several neighbours say their cats won't go out at night at the moment, which made me feel a bit better, as if it's not just Pebble being odd. I've printed posters with her white sock circled. Thank you all, honestly. I'll keep going.

units.author: skeptic_orla
units.text: Cats stay in when it gets cold and still, especially with a frost. It's the most normal cat behaviour there is. Pebble's probably holed up somewhere warm and furious about it. She's going on the overnight show again tonight. The presenter has started calling her 'our Pebble', so we're invested.

units.author: sb_mod
units.text: Pebble's thread stays pinned. I've added a link to it on the Port Ammet page of the board, and printed one of your posters for the newsagent's window on Coopers Yard. Fourteen doors is a lot of doors. Get some sleep.

units.author: sb_bins
units.text: What a private company does with a private island nine kilometres out to sea is none of our business, and frankly none of yours, Gil. Meanwhile there are streets in this town that have not had a recycling collection for three weeks, which is everybody's business. Bernard (Rope Walk)

units.author: truthwatch_gil
units.text: Fine, here's a fact for the planning expert. The officer who signed off ADC/VEG/0917 is a Ms. Varley in Planning, and if you look her up on the professional networking sites she used to work for a consultancy in Halvard. Halvard, where Ardent Vale is registered. I'm not saying anything. I'm asking. Ask her yourself, her email's on the council site.

units.author: sb_mod
units.text: I've removed the post above. It named a council officer and encouraged people to contact her about her previous employment, which is exactly what I asked everyone not to do. If you have evidence of wrongdoing, there is a complaints process and a standards committee. A forum is not either of those. Gil, consider this your one warning.

units.author: skeptic_planner
units.text: Thank you, Pell. For the record, and without names: delegated decisions are signed off under a scheme of delegation, checked by a senior officer, and published with the reasons. Anyone can read the officer's report on this one. It is four pages long and mostly about oil tanks. I've read worse thrillers.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Kit, lad, I said a still day, and you were on the wall with a car stereo. Come out on the boat at six when the water's flat and you'll hear them, a knock and a knock and then the tree going, a long tearing like cloth. Your chippy fan doesn't do the tearing. The clearing's wider again this morning.

units.author: propwatch_ledger
units.text: Small update, as promised: the land registry search has been submitted and I'm told three to five working days. In the meantime, finding 3: the company that the Holm was bought through was dissolved shortly after the sale. That's common with land vehicles, so please don't make anything of it yet. I'll explain why when the search is back.

units.author: hollow_signal
units.text: Some of us have known about the Holm for a long time... The trees aren't the point. The trees were never the point. Ask yourselves what a company like that wants with an island that has nothing on it, and why it has to have nothing on it by a certain date. I can't say more than that. I've already said more than I should.

units.author: skeptic_orla
units.text: Source? To expand, since that's usually all this sort of post deserves: 'I can't say more' is the oldest move on any phone-in. You get the attention for the secret without ever having to have one. The deadline is the contract. It's thirty days because somebody priced it at thirty days. That's all a date is.

units.author: gilliver_teen
units.text: ok fine bram i'll come out at six if you promise not to make me touch a crab. 'a long tearing like cloth' is honestly kind of poetic for a man who once told me my chips were 'an insult to potatoes'

units.title: What is Ardent Vale actually building on the Holm?
units.author: truthwatch_gil
units.text: Starting a proper thread since the other one keeps getting moderated. Facts: island bought through a middleman, middleman dissolved (thanks ledger), council approval with no councillors involved, clearance in a month, owner says nothing. Theories welcome. Mine: some kind of private compound. Rich people want somewhere they can get to and nobody else can. Discuss.

units.author: sb_mod
units.text: Locked. There is already a thread about the Holm clearance and this should go there, within the rules everyone else manages to follow. Duplicate threads make the board harder to read. Also, ledger_lines asked you specifically not to run off with that finding, and you ran off with it within the hour.

units.title: Available now: plant operator, chainsaw tickets, own kit. Port Ammet.
units.author: trades_holm_work
units.text: Davey here, self-employed, available from tomorrow. Tickets: chainsaw maintenance and crosscutting, felling small and large trees, windblown timber, plus 360 excavator and dumper. Own saws, own PPE, own van (it starts, mostly). Storm damage, site clearance, hedges, stumps. No job too small. Day rate negotiable for longer jobs. Island work fine, I've got good sea legs. Port Ammet, Tollinby, Gilliver and anywhere the ferry goes.

units.author: skeptic_brisk
units.text: 'Island work fine.' Subtle, Davey. Grieve aren't reading the Sound Board looking for a man whose van mostly starts. Ring them again. Or come and sell cars, at least ours have wheels on all four corners.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: My mum in Tollinby has a laurel hedge that has eaten half her front path and is coming for the bins. Not glamorous, but it's a full day at least, maybe two, and she makes a very good lunch. Do you do hedges that are basically trees now? I'll message you.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Take the hedge, Davey. It's on the mainland, there's lunch, and you go home to your own bed after. Island work's a different thing in winter. I'm not saying anything against the Holm. I'm saying you can't walk home from it.

units.author: trades_holm_work
units.text: Hedges that are basically trees are my favourite kind of hedge. Message me and I'll come and look this week, free quote. Bram, I hear you. Cal, my van has four wheels, they just don't always agree on the direction.

units.author: wx_carrowpoint
units.text: Yesterday at the Point: max 10.1°C, min -2.3°C, pressure 1026 hPa, wind calm overnight. Coldest night of the autumn so far. Frost on the lantern gallery at dawn, which I could see from my kitchen. Today the wind is going round to the south as promised. Advection fog tonight, I'll stake my rain gauge on it.

edit.text: Yesterday at the Point: max 10.1°C, min 1.3°C (I read the inland sensor column first, the -2.3 was my garden thermometer by the shed, sorry), pressure 1026 hPa, wind calm overnight. Frost on the lantern gallery at dawn, which I could see from my kitchen. Today the wind is going round to the south as promised. Advection fog tonight, I'll stake my rain gauge on it.

units.author: lineman_tess
units.text: Question from the power side: will this be a salty fog? We get salt building up on the insulators along the coast in a long sea fog and then the first drizzle makes it conductive. If you're logging visibility through the week, would you mind if I asked for the numbers later? It'd help us check the patrol notes.

units.author: wx_carrowpoint
units.text: Tess, you can have every number I've got and some I haven't collected yet. A sea fog off water at 11°C will carry salt, yes, particularly near the shore. I've a salt deposition plate on the fence that I wipe weekly; I'll start wiping it daily. Evening reading: visibility 2 km and falling, temperature and dew point both 6.4°C. Here we go.

units.author: lineman_garvey
units.text: Good question, Tess. Salt fog flashover is a real thing, but you need days of it and then a light wetting. One night won't do it. If it sits all week, we'll wash the worst of the coastal insulators. That's the job. Nothing to get excited about yet.

units.author: skeptic_ferrous
units.text: For anyone reading who doesn't speak barometer: when the air cools down to its dew point it can't hold any more water, and the extra shows up as fog. A light southerly over a sea that's still at 11°C does that very efficiently. CarrowPointWx will now be unbearable for a week, and quite right too. He called it two days early.

units.title: Reservoir woods at night.
units.author: brackwater_keeper
units.text: To whoever has been recording in the reservoir woods at night and putting it on the internet: the paths close at dusk and the dam gates are locked overnight. That's estate land, and the banks are steep. As for your knocks, it's deer. Stags clashing, or a buck thrashing a sapling. Rut's not quite done on the estate. I've heard it every autumn for thirty years.

units.author: skeptic_brisk
units.text: Thank you. A man who has actually been in the woods says it's deer. Can we all go home now? Lads, it's deer. Or the wind. It's always deer or the wind.

units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: That's me, and fair on access. I'll ask the estate office properly for permission and stay off the dam end. On the deer: I've got thirty-odd nights of the rut on file from other years, and antler clashes are irregular, with grunting and movement before and after. This was five clean knocks with even spacing and nothing moving within range of the dish. I'm not saying it isn't deer. I'm saying it doesn't sound like the deer I've got.

units.author: lineman_garvey
units.text: I've done night call-outs along the reservoir line for twenty-five years, and a buck thrashing a sapling is a regular whack-whack-whack, I've heard it from the van many a time. The substation transformers also tick when they cool on a frosty night, and that carries over the water. Two ordinary candidates, before anyone gets clever.

units.author: skeptic_orla
units.text: Thank you to everyone who rang the overnight phone-in. Forty-odd calls, which for the overnight show is a stampede. Dunlin played his owls down the line and the presenter went very quiet afterwards and said 'well'. That's the highest praise he gives. Same time next Thursday.

units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: Thanks for having me. You kept your word: nobody asked about anything spooky, and I didn't mention the knocks. It was nice just to play the owls. Tawny pair from the west shore, three weeks ago, minus two and still as anything. Back out tonight if the fog stays out of the valley.

units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: I listened all the way through. The woman who irons tablecloths for the hotel said she can tell which tables had a good evening by the stains. I've been thinking about that for an hour. The owls were lovely. I fell asleep for nearly twenty minutes afterwards, which is a record.

units.title: Re: ferry lost property (the knots book).
units.author: sb_commuter_lisle
units.text: The library book about knots in this week's ferry lost property list is mine. I was trying to learn the bowline so I could stop watching the deckhands do it and feeling inadequate. I am now inadequate and also overdue. I will collect it from the terminal office tomorrow, fog permitting.

units.author: retired_teacher
units.text: Ewan, the rabbit comes up out of the hole, round the tree and back down the hole. I taught that to thirty-four years of children with a skipping rope. I shall teach it to you on the ferry with my scarf if you are not careful.

units.title: School buses in fog?
units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Does anyone know what actually happens with the school buses if the fog's bad tomorrow? The school says 'driver's discretion'. Do they ring? Do they text? Do I stand at the end of the lane with three children and a torch until somebody tells me something? Asking for three children and a torch.

units.author: sb_mod
units.text: In my council days, the school transport office would text parents by 07:15 if a route was cancelled, and the buses ran unless visibility on the route was under about fifty metres. That may have changed. If you've had no text by quarter past seven, assume it's running, but slower.

units.author: sb_roadworks
units.text: Driving the coast road at quarter to five: already thick by the Gilliver turn, maybe sixty metres. Inland's clearer. The school routes are mostly inland, so you'll probably be fine. Dipped lights, fog lights if you've got them, and stay off the back of the car in front.

units.author: dc_3_wendell
units.text: Forty-five seconds. When this building opened, the stair lights were on all night and nobody fell down anything. Then the management company changed three times and somebody in an office decided darkness was cheaper. That is the whole mystery. I will not be discussing it further.

units.author: dc_7_irena
units.text: Dear neighbours, a small report. I went down at seven this morning with Lorna, who kindly knocked for me. The lights went out at seven again, as Mr Tobin says they must. We stood still on the landing together and I counted to ten, and there was nothing at all, only Lorna humming. So I am reassured, and grateful. Irena, 7C

units.author: dc_12_ollie
units.text: kids at school say dellow court has a ghost on the stairs on floor 7 and it follows you down. is that true?? my mum says dont be silly but she also said she doesnt use the stairs after dark which is suspicous. also does anyone know when the lift is fixed

units.author: dellow_admin
units.text: Ollie, hello. Before anything else, is your mum all right with you posting on her account? Just checking, I have to. And no, there is no ghost on the stairs. There is a light timer that is too short and a button on 7 that sticks. Please tell your friends at school that Dellow Court has bad wiring, not ghosts. Bev

units.author: dc_12_ollie
units.text: yes my mum says its fine, she's here, she says hi Bev. ok bad wiring. thats less good to tell people at school tho. Jake from 9 says his brother saw someone on the roof once but Jake also said he met a famous footballer at the chip shop so idk

units.author: dc_8_benedikt
units.text: Something small. Coming home at 21:30 with shopping for 13B, the lights went out between 7 and 8. I stopped to press the button. I heard steps above me, on the flight to 8, and they stopped maybe half a second after I stopped. When the light came on, nobody. Jordie says it is echo. I don't think echo is that late, but I am not an expert in echo. I am only writing it down.

units.author: dc_9_tobin
units.text: On echo timing. 1. Sound travels about 343 m per second. 2. A reflection arriving half a second late has travelled about 170 m, so the surface would be about 85 m away. 3. The whole stairwell is roughly 40 m tall. 4. Echoes in a stairwell this size arrive in tens of milliseconds, not half a second. So whatever Benedikt heard, a simple echo is not the best fit. I am not offering a better fit. I am only doing the sum.

units.author: dc_6_jordie
units.text: ok tobin that is a fun fact i did not want at 11pm. fine. not a simple echo. could be someone on 9 who stopped when they heard Benedikt stop, people do that on dark stairs, you freeze and listen. i do it. it's probably me. i'm probably the ghost. sorry everyone

units.author: dc_8_benedikt
units.text: Jordie, you were in the laundry room at 21:30, I saw your bag of washing by machine 1. So it was not you. Maybe someone on 9, yes. I will ask. Thank you Tobin for the sum.

units.author: dc_2_hassan
units.text: Whatever it is, nobody should be on those stairs with no light. I have torches in the shop now, small ones with a clip, cost price while the lights are bad. Come and ask. Benedikt, there is one behind the counter for you already, no charge, you carry half the building's shopping. H

units.title: Torches at cost price
units.author: dc_2_hassan
units.text: Shop notice. While the lift is out and the stair lights are short, I am selling clip-on torches at cost price. They take two small batteries and clip onto a coat or a bag strap. I have thirty. If you are elderly or have small children, ask and I will put one by for you. Please don't use your phone torch on the stairs and fall. H

units.author: dc_6_jordie
units.text: Hassan the legend strikes again. buying two, one for me and one to clip on Irena's shopping bag. if anyone sees a small light bobbing up the stairs at 2am it's just me going to the shop for noodles

units.author: dellow_admin
units.text: Thank you, Hassan. This is exactly the kind of thing that makes this building bearable. I'll put a note on the noticeboard. I'll also add 'residents are buying their own torches' to the Kerrow email, in bold, in case anyone there still has a conscience. Bev, DCRA

units.author: dc_5_lorna
units.text: I'll take one Hassan love, I've been coming up at five with my phone in my teeth like a dog with a bone, and one for Irena if Jordie hasn't already, she's on my way down anyway, we've made a little arrangement, seven o'clock, I knock twice

units.author: dellow_admin
units.text: Lift update. An engineer came at two, opened the motor room, had a long look, and said the part that's 'in transit' is the wrong part. The right part has now been ordered. He was very nice about it. I was very nice back, for about half a minute. Bev

units.author: dc_3_wendell
units.text: I am told the lift engineer is booked for 'early afternoon'. I shall be in the lobby from half past one with my ring binder, red divider, and I shall be timing him again. Last time he managed four minutes. I am hoping for a personal best.

units.author: dc_3_wendell
units.text: Machine 2 has been eating coins since 2019. There is a note on it. The note says 'out of order'. The note has been there so long it has faded to 'ut of ord'. It is not a mystery. It is a note, and you did not read it.

units.author: dellow_admin
units.text: Adding machine 2 to the Kerrow list, which is now longer than the stairwell. Jordie, I'll ask about refunds, but don't hold your breath. Please nobody try to fix machine 1 yourselves; it's on the same circuit as the ground-floor corridor lights and I'd rather not lose those too.

units.author: dc_6_jordie
units.text: wendell's not wrong. anyone else on the road side getting the work lights straight through the curtains? it's like a ufo has landed in the car park. the planing machine sounds like a giant eating gravel. honestly it's kind of soothing if you pretend it's a documentary about giants

units.author: dc_5_lorna
units.text: the road men were packing up when I got in at five love, lovely smell of hot tar, one of them held the door for me and said 'mind the step it's fresh', which it was, I've got a little black mark on my shoe now like a souvenir

units.author: dc_3_wendell
units.text: Road works outside at night, for anyone who hasn't noticed. I was quoted in the Evening Post this morning as 'a resident of a third-floor flat', and the quote was accurate, which is a first. I said I had heard 'temporary' before, about the lift. They left out the emphasis, but credit where it's due.
units.title: Road works outside (night)

units.author: dc_14_ivy
units.text: From 14 the work lights make the car park look like a stage set (I've sketched it: a row of orange machines, three men in hi-vis, one standing very still looking up at the building, which turned out to be him having a cigarette). The gravel giant is louder up here than you'd think. The riser carries everything.

units.author: lowband_mod
units.text: Pinned. This is what a good post looks like, everyone: raw files from both recorders, kit, gain, rough location, time and conditions, no story attached. Discussion welcome. Ghost-hunting hype is not. If you want to propose an explanation, propose one you could test.

units.author: hobby_hydrophone
units.text: That's a pump. Or a valve. Reservoirs are full of things that clunk on a timer: outflow valves, sump pumps, the gauge house. Sound travels a long way over still water on a frosty night, and a hard metallic knock through a pipe can come out sounding woody after a few hundred metres of trees. Check what's on a timer at the dam.

units.author: skeptic_hollis
units.text: Quick analysis, agreeing with marlo in principle. A valve closing quickly on the outflow main would give you water hammer: a sharp transient, then reflections at intervals set by the pipe length. If the pressure wave bounces between the valve and a junction, you'd get regular repeats. A three-then-two pattern could be two valves. Worth asking the water company when the outflow cycles at night.

units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: Both fair, and testable, which I like. The valve house is at the dam, about 900 m from where I was, with the reservoir between. I've got water hammer from the dam on other files, from when they cycled it in a drought year, and it has a ringing tail after each hit. These don't ring. But I'll write to the water company and ask about their night schedule. If they say 03:40, I'll happily eat my windshield.

units.author: brackwater_keeper
units.text: Posted the same on the Sound Board. It's deer, and you shouldn't be in those woods after dark, son. Estate office is open weekdays if you want permission for daytime recording, which I'd give you. Night recording I won't, not on my patch, not with the banks the way they are this year.

units.author: tern_audio
units.text: ok so spectrogram posted, with arrows (sorry for the arrows). five transients, rise time under 2 ms, most energy between about 800 Hz and 3 kHz, no ringing tail, which I think agrees with dunlin about it not being water hammer? spacing inside the first group 0.58 s and 0.61 s. second group is about 1.5 dB louder on the right-hand omni. that's all I've got. it's a really lovely file.

units.author: skeptic_hollis
units.text: Good spectrogram, arrows forgiven. No ringing tail does weaken my water hammer idea, I'll grant that in one line. It doesn't rule out a mechanical knock somewhere else in the system, or something struck against a trunk. A woody spectrum is consistent with something hitting wood. It doesn't tell us what's doing the hitting.

units.author: hobby_tapeloop
units.text: Dear young man, a very tidy recording, my compliments. It puts me in mind of something in my box of old reels: a tape I made in the seventies when they were doing works on the reservoir dam, with knocking not unlike this, which I always took to be the machinery. I shall look it out, though I warn you my box is not in any order a sane person would recognise. Regards, Ned

units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: Understood, and thank you for the daytime offer, I'll take it. I'll come to the office this week. I've been careful at the dam end, but you know those banks better than I do. For tonight I'm recording from the public footpath on the east side, outside the estate fence, which I believe is allowed. Make of it what you will.

units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: Ned, I'd love to hear that tape whenever it surfaces, in whatever order. Dam works would be a good control: if the old machinery knocks look like these, that's a strong point for the mechanical side. No hurry.

units.author: hobby_binaural
units.text: tern, the louder-on-the-right detail matches what I heard in my headphones last night, which is nice, because I half thought I'd imagined it. So either the source moved right between the groups, or there are two sources. Either is possible with deer, to be fair to the keeper.

units.author: hobby_tapeloop
units.text: Dear tern, not weird at all. The weddings do have speeches. One best man spends four minutes on a story about a goat and never reaches the end, because the tape runs out. I have always wanted to know how it finished. Perhaps that is the true purpose of an archive. Regards, Ned

units.author: tern_audio
units.text: Ned I need to know how the goat story ends. this is my life now. also I'm going out to the reservoir road this week, the bit by the old pumping house, to try and get some of whatever dunlin got. sorry, I mean some owls. and also whatever dunlin got

units.title: Fog week: recording tips?
units.author: hobby_binaural
units.text: The forecast says fog all week. Has anyone recorded in proper sea fog? I've only done Weyhaven in drizzle. I've read that fog deadens the high end and makes distant sounds weirdly clear. headphones on, I'm hoping to do a walk along the estuary road while it's closed for resurfacing. Tips welcome, including 'don't'.

units.author: hobby_hydrophone
units.text: In sea fog at Gilliver you'll hear the Lisle ferry's engines long before you'd expect to, and the horn bounces off everything. Put a bag over your recorder, the moisture gets in. And watch the levels, a horn at 200 m in fog will clip a sensitive mic before you've got your hand to the gain.

units.author: skeptic_hollis
units.text: Fog itself doesn't do much to sound. What does it is the temperature inversion that comes with it: a cool layer near the ground under warmer air bends sound back down instead of letting it escape upward, so distant sources carry. You also lose wind, which helps. The muffled high end is mostly your brain expecting it.

units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: Hollis is right about the inversion. On still nights in the Brack valley you can hear the substation hum from the far side of the reservoir, and trucks on the Tollinby road three kilometres off. In fog it's even more so. Odile, watch your footing on wet tarmac, and wear something bright. Make of it what you will.

units.title: Ward intercom keeps calling a discharged patient
units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: Small one from my break. Our bay intercom keeps calling out a name. Not a staff name: a patient we discharged three weeks ago, a lovely old man who went home to his daughter. It's his bed number and his surname, in the automated voice, about once an hour since midnight. The bed's empty. The call light isn't lit. Maintenance are asleep, like sensible people. Back to it.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: I'd put money on a stuck call button or a fault in the panel that replays the last registered call for that bed. A lot of those systems store the bed's name until someone clears it at the console. When a contact corrodes, the bed 'presses' itself. It's a good night-shift story and a very boring maintenance ticket.

units.author: lh_porter_portammet
units.text: Ours on B corridor did exactly that last winter, kept calling for a bed in Ward 4 that had been moved to Ward 6. Turned out the wall unit had got wet from a leak above the ceiling tiles. Electricians called it 'the haunted bed' for a month and then fixed it in ten minutes. Dmitra's right, I'd say.

units.author: lh_carer_vellmark
units.text: It's horrible when the machines remember someone after they've gone home. We had a door sensor that kept saying 'room 12 open' for a week after a lady moved out. Nobody liked walking past it. I hope your man is doing well at his daughter's.

units.author: hollow_signal
units.text: It isn't the first time a building has remembered a name... and it won't be the last. Some systems are listening for more than their buttons. I won't go into it here. People who know, know.

units.author: lh_mod
units.text: Housekeeping: HollowSignal, this is a nurse on a break telling us about her ward. 'People who know, know' isn't information. Please either say something useful or let her have her break. Ward9, I'd log it for maintenance with the times, so they can match it to the panel's memory.

units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: Logged with the times, thank you all. It did it again at 04:20 while I was reading your replies, and I'll admit I jumped. The charge nurse says a stuck button too and has put a sticky note on the console: 'not him, he's fine, he's at his daughter's'. Ward humour. Back to it.

units.author: lh_security_st
units.text: Follow-up: no van tonight. Same spot at the edge of the lights is empty. I checked the tarmac where it was and there's a small oily patch, so it's a real van with a real leak, which is reassuring in a stupid way. If it comes back I'll knock on the window, as promised. Control says I've 'got a thing about that van'. Control is right.

units.author: lh_dockguard_coriveth
units.text: Oil patch noted. Good detail. If it returns: time, position relative to the patch, exhaust yes or no. A pattern is more use than a feeling. I have had a thing about a forklift for two years. It is just a forklift.

units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: night three, callers so far: a man who wanted to know if his electricity was 'the green kind' (it isn't); a woman reporting a flickering street light who then talked to me for nine minutes about her sister; and the meter man, who read his meter, said 'same as yesterday, more or less', and wished me a quiet night. I love him. I will never meet him.

units.author: lh_kennel_orrin
units.text: 'Same as yesterday, more or less' is honestly how I'd describe every night here too. Except tonight Pickle the beagle ate a tea towel and is now very proud and slightly unwell. Nothing a vet hospital can't handle. Being next door to one is the best part of this job.

units.author: lh_trucker_orrin
units.text: The street light lady with the sister, that's the call that matters, darlin'. Folk ring a helpline at three in the morning because it's the only number that answers. You did nine minutes of good work there and your supervisor will log it as 'lamp, flickering'.

units.author: lh_trucker_orrin
units.text: Thank you, doc. 'A brain doing its best with too little' is going on a sticker in my cab. Last night between mileposts 180 and 200 I did the full routine: pulled in, coffee, twenty minutes, walked round the rig twice. Woke up properly for the first time in a week. Never felt so smug in my life.

units.author: lh_taxi_halvard
units.text:
I tried the coffee then nap thing at the rank
woke up to a fare knocking on the window
he'd been waiting four minutes
tipped me anyway because he said I 'looked peaceful'
anyway it works

units.title: What's your 3am snack?
units.author: lh_baker_coriveth
units.text: Bakery question while the croissants rest. What do you eat at 3am? I have an unfair advantage: tonight it's the end of a cardamom bun, still warm, torn in half and eaten standing over the bench. Before I worked here it was crackers and cheese in front of the fridge, which I still think is the best way to eat crackers.

units.author: lh_porter_portammet
units.text: Toast from the ward toaster that doesn't exist, obviously. Failing that, a packet of the cheese crackers from machine 3, eaten in the lift between floors with the doors shut. Best two minutes of the night.

units.author: lh_carer_vellmark
units.text: An apple, cut into slices, shared with whichever resident is awake. Tonight it's a gentleman who used to be a station master and tells me the times of trains that haven't run for fifty years. He takes the slices very seriously, one at a time, as if they were tickets.

units.author: lh_picker_weyhaven
units.text: cold pasta from a tub, eaten with the lid as a spoon because I forgot a fork again. the shrine was out of egg sandwiches. it is always out of egg sandwiches. the scanner pinged at me while I was eating, like it was judging

units.author: dc_5_lorna
units.text: a custard cream dunked in the urn tea love, which is a crime against custard creams but it's tradition at the depot, the drivers start arriving at half four and we all have one together before the buses go out, like a little congregation

units.title: Best view you get on shift?
units.author: lh_crane_halvard
units.text: Light one to get people talking. Mine's obvious: sixty metres up over Halvard, with the whole ring road lit and the river black through the middle. On a clear night I can see the airport lights to the north. What's yours? Doesn't have to be pretty. Just has to be yours.

units.author: lh_miner_vellmark
units.text: Rock. Wet rock, lit by my cap lamp, about a metre in front of my face. Then at the end of the shift, the cage comes up and you see the sky over the headframe going grey. That's the view. It's a good one, when it comes.

units.author: lh_lighttender_tamsin
units.text: From the lantern gallery, the beam going round, and in each pass a few seconds of sea, then the headland, then the road along the cliff, then sea again. You learn the landscape in slices. On some nights I know where every gate and post is along that road by the way the light finds it. I like to think the light knows them too.

units.author: lh_security_st
units.text: Twelve CCTV screens in the hut, each one a different empty bit of car park. It's not pretty, but at four in the morning when the cleaners' van comes in, all twelve screens get a little bit of life at once. Feels like a tiny sunrise.

units.author: lh_student_kestrel
units.text: update: banana stage confirmed. also chapter three now has a first paragraph, which my supervisor will describe as 'a start'. the cleaner who hums brought me a sweet and said 'nearly there' in the exact tone of someone who has seen many theses die. thank you for the support, 24h. I bought two bananas.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Prices today. Cod 4.25, haddock 3.70, langoustine good, crab finally up a bit. Wind gone south, light. Glass falling slow. Mist on the water by four, thick by the Holm side already. Brought the creels in early, I'll not be out in the morning if it's what I think it is. Plenty of folk in the chandlery buying horns.

units.author: harbour_admin
units.text: sold eleven fog horns today lads. eleven. I've been here twenty two years and that's a record. two of them were to the same man who forgot he'd already bought one in the morning. sold out of the good torches too, more coming tuesday

units.author: harbourmaster_quill
units.text: Rook's two battery lamps are now at the foot of the Gilliver slip, chained to the rail, thank you Rook. I'll switch them on at dusk and off at the first boat. The permanent fittings are on order. Please, nobody fish from the bottom of the slip tonight; with the fog coming in, the ferry crew won't see you until they're on top of you.

units.author: ferry_mate_kerris
units.text: Thanks Quill. The lamps make a real difference, I could see them from a cable off last night before the fog. Bottom of the slip is still black at the edges where the light doesn't reach, but at least we can see where the water starts. That's the bit that matters.

units.author: deckhand_finn
units.text: confirmed the lamps are class, did my controlled slide last night under proper lighting, very dignified, nobody saw except kerris and the skipper and three passengers and a dog. fog tonight though, I've got two jumpers and the good gloves and a flask of tea that my mum calls 'soup'

units.title: Fog procedure (crew, please read)
units.author: ferry_skipper_odell
units.text: Fog advisory from 22:00. Reminder for the late Gilliver run: radar watch on the bridge, one lookout forward at all times, sound signal every two minutes, speed at the skipper's discretion, which means slow. Nobody goes to the bottom of a slip without a torch and a second person. If anyone sees anything they can't identify, report it to the bridge, don't shout it across the deck. We log it and we carry on.

units.author: ferry_engineer_seth
units.text: Below will be ready. Both gensets checked, the sulky one included, and the forward flood rewired so it doesn't share a circuit with the galley kettle any more. You can now have tea and light at the same time. Progress.

units.author: ferry_mate_kerris
units.text: Read and understood, skipper. Lookout forward, loud-hailer by the wheelhouse door, good torch charged. I'll do the first lookout. Last fog week we nearly hit a creel buoy off Lisle because somebody was looking at his phone. I won't say who.

units.author: deckhand_finn
units.text: it was me. it was me looking at my phone. I've said sorry to that buoy. I'll do second lookout and I'll leave my phone in my locker like a monk. if I see 'anything I can't identify' I promise to report it calmly to the bridge and not scream it across the deck like last time with the seal

units.author: lisle_crew_ada
units.text: Lisle pier will have all lights on and I'll ring the bell when I hear you coming... ha, like the old days. If I can't hear your horn I'll assume you're still out there and wait. I always wait. Safe crossing tonight, all of you.

units.author: ferry_engineer_seth
units.text: Garvey, while you're being prophetic, can you prophesy me a fuel filter? The number two genset dipped the deck floods twice on the late crossing. Not dangerous, just irritating, and some of the passengers think it's spooky, which is worse for business than irritating.

units.author: lineman_garvey
units.text: Filters are your department, Seth. Prophecy costs extra and comes with a flaming long wait, like everything else in this co-op. What I can tell you is the Quay Row blip at two o'clock today was us switching at Brackwater, not your genset, in case any of your passengers in the harbour cafe thought the lights were spooky too.

units.author: lineman_tess
units.text: Four minutes on Quay Row, I timed it from the switching log. Sorry, harbour. The substation inspection's done now and it's officially boring, which Garvey says is the best grade there is. Next week we're washing the coastal insulators if the fog hangs about, so you'll see us on the poles by the boatyard.

units.author: harbour_admin
units.text: Holm boat skipper came in this morning and bought a fog horn and a box of flares, says he'll run tomorrow if he can see the end of the wall and not if he can't. sensible man. told me the camp on the island looks 'tidy'. that's all he'd say. he's not a talker lads, leave him be

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Good. That's the right rule for fog round the Holm side. The tide runs hard past their landing at springs, and there's the old curing station piles under the water off the north end, if you don't know them. I've told him where they are. He wrote it on his hand.

units.author: lisle_crew_ada
units.text: Lisle pier, evening... mist coming in over the slip already, the far end of the pier is soft at the edges. 17:50 in on time. Margaret the goat didn't travel today, I was a bit disappointed, ha. Lights all working. Bell polished. Feels like the start of something, the first fog of the year. Anyway.

units.author: lh_dockguard_coriveth
units.text: Gate 7: floodlit stacks, rows of containers, red, blue and rust, with the cranes standing over them like herons. At about 04:00 the first inbound ship's lights appear at the breakwater and the whole yard starts to move. That is the view. Logged as: good.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Professional answer: something small with a bit of protein, because a big carbohydrate meal at 3am makes the 5am slump worse. Personal answer: one boiled egg and three salted almonds, eaten in front of a wall of sleeping patients' brainwaves. I am aware of how that sounds.

units.author: gilliver_teen
units.text: told him bram. he said and i quote 'tell Bram the chips are the same chips his father ate and his father never complained'. then he said 'actually his father complained every week'. so i think that means you're both right. haddock's on again thursday

units.author: gilliver_lamp
units.text: Dear, I had a cat called Moss who went missing for nine days in a fog the winter my husband retired, and came home fatter than he left, so somebody somewhere had been feeding him very well. Keep the blanket on the step and the light on in the kitchen. They like to see the house is awake.

units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: I've set aside two tickets for the first night behind my counter in an envelope marked 'Mrs Hale, for the blue river'. It seems only fair. A hundred and six gone so far. The poetry shelf has never seen so much foot traffic.
